title: Expert: Handle plugin ABI breakage between 4.6.0 and 4.6.1.
description:
Commit 5d49f6ca added the "same_name_next" field to the expert_field_info
structure, inadvertently breaking plugin ABI and leading to crashes inside
expert_register_field_array when the plugin build version and the application
version weren't identical.

Exploit the default value of eiinfo.hf_info.hfinfo.(id|parent) to determine
whether each structure we receive was built for 4.6.0 or 4.6.1-or-later, and
adjust behavior accordingly, fixing up accesses to hf_info and redirecting
accesses to same_name_next.  This isn't very clean, but it does mean we should
be able to run with plugins built against either 4.6.0 or 4.6.1-or-newer.

Fixes #20881.

Fixup 5d49f6ca.

I've tested this on both Linux (GCC and Clang) and macOS (Clang) and confirmed that it can load plugins built with 4.6.0 or 4.6.1 or with latest release-4.6.

I have not tested on Windows.  If someone could run a quick test for me, building the plugins with 4.6.0 and 4.6.1 and checking that they are successfully loaded with this fix on release-4.6, that'd be awesome.  A super quick test is to just run "tshark -G plugins".  Running the whole pytest test suite (with the 4.6.0 plugins and again with the 4.6.1 plugins) is another option.

@dariusd0 IMO this approach can't work because in 5d49f6ca521ddcd516eeb7d5425d4a5d51bf41cb the size of the public `expert_field_info` struct changed. If a plugin keeps them in an array the second struct will be off. Size of public structs can't change without breaking ABI.

The only way is returning to the original (4.6.0) size of the struct and finding a new fix for the original problem.

Thanks for the feedback, @rbalint!

I think I've already taken care of your concern by computing a `stride` value at runtime according to the ABI revision detected.

The value of `stride` is determined (at line 529) based upon the contents of the first element of the array (line 499), solely based upon memory accesses which fit within the bounds of the minimal single-element input array of the smallest accepted type -- so they should be "safe" for any valid input, regardless of the ABI used.

The computed `stride` value is then used to correctly locate the position of array members subsequent to the first (line 533-534).

Wireshark includes several plugins which register an array with multiple expert info members, e.g. `plugins/epan/wimaxasncp/packet-wimaxasncp.c`:

```
3258     static ei_register_info ei[] = {
3259         { &ei_wimaxasncp_tlv_type, { "wimaxasncp.tlv.type.unknown", PI_UNDECODED, PI_WARN, "Unknown tlv", EXPFILL }},
3260         { &ei_wimaxasncp_function_type, { "wimaxasncp.function_type.unknown", PI_UNDECODED, PI_WARN, "Unknown function type", EXPFILL }},
3261         { &ei_wimaxasncp_op_id, { "wimaxasncp.opid.unknown", PI_UNDECODED, PI_WARN, "Unknown message op", EXPFILL }},
3262         { &ei_wimaxasncp_decoder, { "wimaxasncp.decoder.unknown", PI_UNDECODED, PI_WARN, "Unknown decoder", EXPFILL }},
3263         { &ei_wimaxasncp_message_type, { "wimaxasncp.message_type.unknown", PI_UNDECODED, PI_WARN, "Unknown message type", EXPFILL }},
3264         { &ei_wimaxasncp_length_bad, { "wimaxasncp.length.bad", PI_MALFORMED, PI_ERROR, "Bad length", EXPFILL }},
3265     };
[...]
3318     expert_register_field_array(expert_wimaxasncp, ei, array_length(ei));
```

Those appear to be correctly handled with the fix in this commit.

Please let me know if your concern is not addressed (pun not intended :grin:) by the above.

How about this?

```
static ei_register_info ei[] = {
3259         { &ei_wimaxasncp_tlv_type, { "wimaxasncp.tlv.type.unknown", PI_UNDECODED, PI_WARN, "Unknown tlv", EXPFILL }},
3260         { &ei_wimaxasncp_function_type, { "wimaxasncp.function_type.unknown", PI_UNDECODED, PI_WARN, "Unknown function type", EXPFILL }},
3261         { &ei_wimaxasncp_op_id, { "wimaxasncp.opid.unknown", PI_UNDECODED, PI_WARN, "Unknown message op", EXPFILL }},
3262         { &ei_wimaxasncp_decoder, { "wimaxasncp.decoder.unknown", PI_UNDECODED, PI_WARN, "Unknown decoder", EXPFILL }},
3263         { &ei_wimaxasncp_message_type, { "wimaxasncp.message_type.unknown", PI_UNDECODED, PI_WARN, "Unknown message type", EXPFILL }},
3264         { &ei_wimaxasncp_length_bad, { "wimaxasncp.length.bad", PI_MALFORMED, PI_ERROR, "Bad length", EXPFILL }},
3265     };
[...]
3318     expert_register_field_array(expert_wimaxasncp), &(ei[1]), array_length(ei) - 1);

```

I don't see how that could cause any problem.  `&(ei[i])` is still a valid pointer to the start of a `struct ei_register_info`, and `array_length(ei) - 1` is the valid and correct length of the remainder of the array.

`stride` will still be correctly determined based upon the contents of `ei[1]`, and that will be used to locate the rest of the items, starting at the given address (`&(ei[1])`), with the stride suitable for whichever ABI was used when the code was compiled.

`ei[0]` won't get registered, but the rest of the `ei` array should be correctly registered.

@dariusd0 if sizeof(struct ei_register_info) changes, and the plugin is compiled with sizeof1, then the plugin passes ei + sizeof1 to the library that could only work if the passed pointer would be ei + sizeof2.

We can add heuristic validity checks to find plugins compiled against 4.6.1 and showing an error to recompile them against 4.6.0. They would work most of the time, but this approach with looking at the first array element does not prevent all unlikely but valid ABI usages from crashing.

> if sizeof(struct ei_register_info) changes, and the plugin is compiled with sizeof1, then the plugin passes ei + sizeof1 to the library that could only work if the passed pointer would be ei + sizeof2

I don't follow.  With the modification as you gave above:

If the plugin is built against 4.6.0, the modified plugin will pass in `ei + sizeof ei_register_info_4_6_0`, which will always be the valid start of a `struct ei_register_info_4_6_0`, regardless of which version of Wireshark it is run against, because the size of each array element in the compiled object is `sizeof ei_register_info_4_6_0`.

If the plugin is built against 4.6.1, the modified plugin will pass in `ei + sizeof ei_register_info_4_6_1`, which will always be the valid start of a `struct ei_register_info_4_6_1`, regardless of which version of Wireshark it is run against, because the size of each array element in the compiled object is `sizeof ei_register_info_4_6_1`.

A gdb log might help explain things.

The `../choose-plugins.sh` referenced below is a short shell script I use when debugging this issue.  It is used to select which plugins to run with.  It can accept `4.6.0`, `4.6.1` and `release-4.6` for the respective released version tags or the release branch, and also `4.6.0-modified` and `4.6.1-modified` with your modification to pass in `ei[1]` when `register_wimaxasncp_fields` calls `expert_register_field_array`.

If the concern is whether plugins built against 4.6.2+ should run against 4.6.0 but crash on 4.6.1 (versus running on 4.6.1 and crashing on 4.6.0, as they currently will with this MR), then I can remove the `saved_same_name` field from expert.h again – it is truly unused – and then any plugins built against future 4.6.x will be backwards compatible with 4.6.0, but will crash only on 4.6.1.
You mean remove `same_name_next` from `expert_field_info`? Yes this would restore the ABI to 4.6.0's and this is what I believe the right path.

Yeah, I meant remove `same_name_next`.

If that will alleviate your concern, I'll happily remove it from `expert.h` and flip the logic in `expert.c` to special case 4.6.1 instead of special-casing 4.6.0 as it does now.

The only way I can see for the `&(ei[1])` thing could become a concern would be in the case of a single plugin which is built from components themselves compiled against a _mixture_ of ABIs, with one of those components (on one ABI) producing an `expert_field_info` array and the other (on another ABI) manipulating the `expert_field_info` array pointer using a different size.  This is not impossible... but seems unlikely.  The MR, as it stands now, should be robust for a plugin built against any single ABI but can't do anything about the plugin-with-internally-mixed-ABI case.  Removing `same_name_next` and flipping the logic in `expert.c` to special-case 4.6.1 would minimize (but can not eliminate) the risk of failure from an internally-mixed-ABI plugin simply because it is less likely that a mixed-ABI build will incorporate 4.6.1 than 4.6.0 or latest-4.6.x.

Does that sound like an agreeable plan?

Or do you think the attempt to achieve backwards-compatibility by examining the structure's contents is just too smelly?  (I freely admit it is smelly...)

commits_data.title: Expert: Handle plugin ABI breakage between 4.6.0 and 4.6.1.
commits_data.message:
Expert: Handle plugin ABI breakage between 4.6.0 and 4.6.1.

Commit 5d49f6ca added the "same_name_next" field to the expert_field_info
structure, inadvertently breaking plugin ABI and leading to crashes inside
expert_register_field_array when the plugin build version and the application
version weren't identical.

Exploit the default value of eiinfo.hf_info.hfinfo.(id|parent) to determine
whether each structure we receive was built for 4.6.0 or 4.6.1-or-later, and
adjust behavior accordingly, fixing up accesses to hf_info and redirecting
accesses to same_name_next.  This isn't very clean, but it does mean we should
be able to run with plugins built against either 4.6.0 or 4.6.1-or-newer.

Fixes #20881.
Fixup 5d49f6ca.
